evidence.title: Securing Collaborative Medical AI by Using Differential Privacy: Domain Transfer for Classification of Chest Radiographs
evidence.outcome: Effect of differential privacy on cross-institutional diagnostic AUC and subgroup performance versus non-DP models
evidence.effect: At ε≈1, no evidence of AUC differences between DP-DT and non-DP-DT; subgroup AUC differences under 1% for sex subgroups and nearly all age subgroups. Privacy protection itself was not measured.
evidence.quote: Cross-institutional performance of artificial intelligence models was not affected by DP.

evidence.title: Privacy-by-Design Approach to Generate Two Virtual Clinical Trials for Multiple Sclerosis and Release Them as Open Datasets: Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Protection against distance-based membership inference attacks and other privacy metrics in synthetic datasets
evidence.effect: Membership inference protection was hardest privacy metric to optimize but yielded robust privacy; selected datasets had hidden rates of 85.0% and 93.2%.
evidence.quote: Protection against membership inference attacks was the hardest privacy metric to optimize, but the technique yielded robust privacy and replication of the primary end points (in 72.5% and 80.8% of the 1080 generated datasets).
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic datasets generated from two multiple sclerosis RCTs (n=865 and 1516 patients)

evidence.title: DPF-CM: A Data Processing Framework with Privacy-Preserving Vector Databases for Chinese Medical LLMs Training and Deployment
evidence.outcome: Training data privacy leakage with the Privacy Preserving Vector Database approach
evidence.effect: The framework reduces training data privacy leakage by 27%.
evidence.quote: Moreover, the framework reduces training data privacy leakage by 27%.

evidence.title: How to Train Private Clinical Language Models: A Comparative Study of Privacy-Preserving Pipelines for ICD-9 Coding
evidence.outcome: Membership-inference AUC and ICD-9 coding utility across differentially private training pipelines
evidence.effect: Knowledge distillation from DP-trained teachers recovered up to 63% of non-private performance at epsilon 4 and 6 with membership-inference AUC approximately 0.5, outperforming direct DP-SGD and DP-synthetic data.
evidence.quote: At moderate and relaxed privacy budgets ($\varepsilon \in \{4, 6\}$), knowledge distillation from DP-trained teachers outperforms both direct DP-SGD and DP-synthetic data training, recovering up to 63\% of the non-private performance whilst maintaining strong empirical privacy (membership-inference AUC $\approx$ 0.5).

evidence.title: MedPriv-Bench: Benchmarking the Privacy-Utility Trade-off of Large Language Models in Medical Open-Ended Question Answering
evidence.outcome: Privacy leakage and clinical utility of LLMs with vs without privacy-preserving methods
evidence.effect: Unprotected Med42-v2-8B: utility 3.87/5, leakage 72.8%. Supervised fine-tuning: utility 4.25, leakage 38.9%. Local differential privacy: leakage 20.5%, utility 3.03.
evidence.quote: Relative to unprotected Med42-v2-8B (utility 3.87/5; leakage 72.8%), supervised fine-tuning improved utility to 4.25 and reduced leakage to 38.9%, whereas local differential privacy reduced leakage to 20.5% but lowered utility to 3.03.

evidence.title: ProtoMedAgent: Multimodal Clinical Interpretability via Privacy-Aware Agentic Workflows
evidence.outcome: Artifact-level membership inference risk with the semantic privacy gate
evidence.effect: The l-diversity phase transition reduced artifact-level membership inference risk by an absolute 9.8%.
evidence.quote: ProtoMedAgent additionally leverages a binding $\ell$-diversity phase transition to systematically reduce artifact-level membership inference risks by an absolute 9.8%.

evidence.title: FedIHRAS: A Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Framework for Multi-Institutional Collaborative Radiological Analysis with Integrated Explainability and Automated Clinical Reporting
evidence.outcome: Resistance of federated model with differential privacy to inference and reconstruction attacks
evidence.effect: Privacy robustness tests reported strong resistance against inference and reconstruction attacks; no attack success rates given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Moreover, privacy robustness tests confirm strong resistance against inference and reconstruction attacks.
evidence.sample_unit: chest radiograph images (approximate, across four datasets)

evidence.title: Membership Disclosure Evaluation for Synthetic Clinical Text Generated by LLM via Dynamic Few-Shot In-Context Learning
evidence.outcome: Membership inference attack success on synthetic clinical text under static vs dynamic few-shot ICL
evidence.effect: Static 1-shot ICL showed high membership disclosure risk; static 2-3 shots markedly reduced risk; dynamic ICL kept F1 near chance with M approx 0 or slightly negative across all k.
evidence.quote: Dynamic ICL consistently suppresses disclosure across all $k$, with F1 near chance and $M \approx 0$ or slightly negative, signifying negligible exploitable signal.

evidence.title: Privacy Preserving Disease Prediction Across Multiple Hospitals Using CKKS Based Homomorphic Federated Learning
evidence.outcome: Membership-inference attack AUC with encrypted aggregation versus plaintext federated learning
evidence.effect: HE-FL reduced membership-inference attack performance to random-guess level (AUC = 0.5000); utility fell to F1 = 0.4042, ROC-AUC = 0.7714 vs plaintext F1 = 0.9922, ROC-AUC = 0.9996.
evidence.quote: the proposed HE-FL configuration retained meaningful predictive capability (F1 = 0.4042; ROC-AUC = 0.7714) and reduced membership-inference attack performance to the random-guess level (AUC = 0.5000) under the evaluated protocol.

evidence.title: Impact of differential privacy on breast ultrasound image classification performance using vision transformer
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy, F1 and AUC-ROC of ViT-B/16 with versus without differential privacy across epsilon/delta settings
evidence.effect: Without DP: 94.9% accuracy, 93.4% F1, 99.2% AUC. With DP at ε=10, δ=1e-5: 89.5%, 86.0%, 96.1%. At ε=0.01: 48.3%, 43.5%, 48.6%. Privacy leakage itself was not measured.
evidence.quote: A clinically viable compromise emerged at ε=1, δ=0.1 (87.4% accuracy, 82.8% F1, 94.1% AUC-ROC).

evidence.title: An adaptive differential privacy framework for clinical llms with context-aware noise calibration, hierarchical budgeting, and real-time auditing
evidence.outcome: Membership inference risk reduction with differential privacy and privacy auditing in clinical LLM
evidence.effect: Mitigated membership inference risk by 65.9% versus state-of-the-art privacy-preserving LLMs; utility-privacy trade-off improved 15.8% at ε=0.1, δ=10⁻⁶.
evidence.quote: By improving the utility–privacy trade-off by 15.8%, mitigating membership inference risk by 65.9%, and reducing computational overhead by 23.4%, the framework establishes a more secure, efficient, and trustworthy foundation for clinical AI deployment.
evidence.sample_unit: documents/records (MIMIC-III 2.1M documents, i2b2 858K records, proprietary hospital dataset 1.5M records)

evidence.title: Security Analysis of a Federated Learning Framework for Medical Image-to-Image Translation
evidence.outcome: Membership inference AUC with vs without Secure Aggregation
evidence.effect: FedMIA AUC 0.92-0.99 without SecAgg; SecAgg reduced AUC to 0.23, 0.46, 0.56, 0.54 for Centers A-D with negligible impact on synthesis quality.
evidence.quote: The implementation of SecAgg substantially reduced the attack efficacy, as evidenced by the AUC values, which decreased to 0.23, 0.46, 0.56, and 0.54 for Centers A, B, C, and D, respectively (see Fig. 3 ).

evidence.title: Shareable artificial intelligence to extract cancer outcomes from electronic health records for precision oncology research
evidence.outcome: Vulnerability of text classifiers trained on PHI to membership inference attacks
evidence.effect: Membership inference vulnerability was confirmed in text classification models trained directly on PHI. Teacher-student distillation onto public MIMIC-IV data was used to build shareable models.
evidence.quote: In this study, the vulnerability of text classification models trained directly on protected health information to membership inference attacks is confirmed.
evidence.sample_unit: documents (imaging reports, oncologist notes, discharge summaries)

evidence.title: The Model's Language Matters: A Comparative Privacy Analysis of LLMs
evidence.outcome: Privacy leakage via extraction, counterfactual memorization, and membership inference across four languages
evidence.effect: Privacy vulnerability scales with linguistic redundancy and tokenization granularity; Italian shows strongest leakage, English higher membership separability, French and Spanish more resilient.
evidence.quote: Results show that privacy vulnerability scales with linguistic redundancy and tokenization granularity: Italian exhibits the strongest leakage, while English shows higher membership separability.

evidence.title: Exploring Membership Inference Vulnerabilities in Clinical Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Membership inference leakage of patient records from fine-tuned clinical LLM using loss-based and paraphrase-based attacks
evidence.effect: Limited but measurable membership leakage; the clinical LLM showed partial resistance but remained susceptible to subtle privacy risks. No numeric results reported in the text.
evidence.quote: Our preliminary findings reveal limited but measurable membership leakage, suggesting that current clinical LLMs provide partial resistance yet remain susceptible to subtle privacy risks that could undermine trust in clinical AI adoption.

evidence.title: Fidelity, Diversity, and Privacy: A Multi-Dimensional LLM Evaluation for Clinical Data Augmentation
evidence.outcome: Privacy/plagiarism (memorization) of LLM-generated synthetic mental health reports
evidence.effect: All three models reportedly generated privacy-safe synthetic reports, with no compromise of patient confidentiality; no numeric results given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The results demonstrate that all models can generate clinically coherent, diverse, and privacy-safe synthetic reports, significantly expanding the available training data for clinical natural language processing tasks without compromising patient confidentiality.

evidence.title: Reconstruction of Personally Identifiable Information from Proprietary Data in Supervised Fine-Tuned Models
evidence.outcome: Targeted PII reconstruction from LLMs fine-tuned on small proprietary medical and legal SFT data
evidence.effect: COVA consistently improves PII reconstruction over baseline decoding methods across datasets. Even limited contextual knowledge about a target user substantially increases adversary success.
evidence.quote: Our findings demonstrate that small, proprietary SFT datasets can induce meaningful privacy leakage through the reconstruction of target-PII associations learned during fine-tuning.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic multi-turn Q&A datasets (medical and legal)

evidence.title: A novel gradient inversion attack framework to investigate privacy vulnerabilities during retinal image-based federated learning
evidence.outcome: Identification of training participants from reconstructed retinal images via gradient inversion attack in federated learning
evidence.effect: Across all models, over 92% of training-set participants could be identified from reconstructed retinal vessel structure alone; with differential privacy, substantial information could still be extracted.
evidence.quote: Experimental results for the task of retinal age prediction demonstrate that, across all models, over 92 % of the participants in the training set could be identified from their reconstructed retinal vessel structure alone.

evidence.title: Memorization in large language models in medicine prevalence characteristics and implications
evidence.outcome: Prevalence and persistence of training-data memorization, including sensitive clinical content, in medical LLMs
evidence.effect: Memorization was prevalent and significantly higher than in the general domain; up to 87% of content memorized during continued pretraining remained after fine-tuning; harmful memorization included sensitive clinical content.
evidence.quote: The results demonstrate that memorization is prevalent and significantly higher than that in the general domain.
evidence.sample_unit: inpatient records (Yale New Haven Health System, over 13,000 unique records)

commentary.bottom_line: Eleven benchmark and simulation studies suggest that differential privacy, secure or encrypted aggregation, and related methods can lower membership inference success, often at a measurable cost to model accuracy. No study tested these methods or privacy red-teaming in a deployed clinical system, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: Eleven studies test privacy-enhancing methods. All are automated benchmarks or simulations, and one is rated level 4. Nine report reduced membership inference or leakage, and two report mixed results. Outcomes are simulated attack metrics rather than observed re-identification. The methods differ too widely to pool, so certainty is very low.

Hazard studies show the risk exists. Over 92% of training participants were identified from reconstructed retinal images, and up to 87% of memorized content persisted after fine-tuning. In tests, secure aggregation lowered attack AUC from 0.92-0.99 to 0.23-0.56, and encrypted aggregation reached 0.5000. Differential privacy alone still allowed substantial extraction in the retinal study.

Protection often came at a utility cost. Encrypted federated learning lowered F1 from 0.9922 to 0.4042. Differential privacy reduced breast ultrasound accuracy from 94.9% to 89.5% at ε=10 and to 48.3% at ε=0.01, without measuring leakage. Local differential privacy cut LLM leakage to 20.5% but lowered utility to 3.03 from 3.87. Distillation recovered up to 63% of non-private performance.

One test, a Chinese benchmark, used non-English data and reported a 27% reduction in leakage. A hazard study across four languages found that leakage varied by language, with Italian showing the most. This suggests that results from English data may not carry over. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors using differential privacy to document trade-offs with accuracy and utility. NIST AI 600-1 calls for red-teaming for membership inference. The accuracy results across epsilon settings and the utility losses under encrypted aggregation show the kind of trade-off data such documentation may require. No study evaluated red-teaming as a governance process.

commentary.research_gap: No study measured re-identification events in deployed clinical AI systems. No study compared organizations that conduct privacy red-teaming with those that do not. No study reported the cost, staffing, or time needed to run these assessments. Studies are also needed that use standard attack protocols so that results across methods can be compared and pooled.
commentary.underserved_note: One test used Chinese-language data, and no test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. A hazard study found that leakage differs by language, so protection levels measured on English or single-language data may not apply to records from patients with limited English proficiency or to multilingual safety-net settings.
